name: Tomas Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI companies, employers, unions, parties and government; we don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, including what you'd only say here. What is your usual working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage six people at the order desk of a large seed company. We check germination certificates, schedule spring deliveries and answer growers who want a different variety after an order is packed. I have a bachelor's degree and have done this for eight years; I'm competent at the usual cases, less sure when weather and stock both change overnight. I use AI every day for the first delivery plan, then ring the warehouse to check what's really there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what is pressing at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like hearing a grower say the replacement seed arrived before planting day. I'm 43 and live with my wife Salma and our children, nine and thirteen, in a mortgaged house. Salma cooks at a restaurant; her shifts vary, and my manager wage is low for this work. We have about three weeks of expenses saved after replacing the boiler. There are few other seed offices nearby, so I can't just walk into the same post across town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would still use the planning tool for the first pass, and people would still sort out late seed with growers. I can handle that. The boiler payment and Salma's uneven shifts would still have us checking the account each Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to compare the AI delivery list with the bags in the warehouse. I'd tell Salma the order desk probably stays busy. I wouldn't make a grand claim that a faster list will fix a late truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm relieved about the job but not calm about our money. Three weeks of expenses will disappear in a bad month, and the mortgage is due whether planting is busy or quiet. I already earn less than many managers, and there are few similar desks here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this week I'd keep asking the warehouse lead to confirm the top ten orders before we promise delivery. Through the first year of a plateau, I'd keep our existing AI first pass and cancel two takeaway meals a month, putting the saved 30 toward a one-month cash buffer. If Salma loses shifts, we'd pause the transfer and keep the mortgage and food paid first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about ordinary bills, even with no big AI change. The quiet picture doesn't fix a thin bank account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the top ten list is wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the tool said there were forty bags of early peas, but twenty were reserved for another farm. The warehouse lead caught it before I promised them. A seed bag on a screen cannot fill a planter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can thirty a month really build a buffer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly, if Salma gets her usual shifts. I won't pretend thirty makes us safe next month. It is one cut the children barely notice.

I'd tell Salma the desk should stay **busy with growers** if change stays small.
think: I'm relieved about work but **anxious about money** with only three weeks saved.

Cancel **two monthly takeaways**; save 30 only if Salma's usual shifts hold and both wages cover mortgage and food.
feel: I feel **anxious** about bills despite a steady order desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing order replies, checking certificates, planning lorries and answering growers are my team's whole day. Stronger AI could take a lot of that before robots do any loading. I use tools readily, but six desk posts may become three even if I manage the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team we need to test the system on bad stock days, not only the neat weeks. I'd ask our director for the planned number of desk posts in writing. To growers I'd promise a person for a disputed substitution, not a perfect machine answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be one of the three who go; I've been here eight years, but I'm not the best certificate reader. My quick use of AI could help me lead a pilot, yet it could also show the director we need fewer people. Salma's wage would not carry our mortgage if mine stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I'd run a paid four-week trial on last spring's missed deliveries if the director approves, and learn the new certificate checks with my senior clerk. If it works, I'd use AI only for routine order replies while a person checks substitutions before a lorry leaves. I'd stop the children's extra streaming package and keep the saved money in cash while the staffing number is unsettled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own desk and the six people I supervise. I can help test the tool, but I can't promise what the director does with the result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which worker worries you first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My senior clerk Ina knows which certificate is missing before I do. She deserves a chance at any remaining job, even if that means she beats me to it. I'd tell her the trial results as soon as I have them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say publicly that the pilot might cut you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not to customers. I would tell staff privately that the staffing number could fall, and I would ask for the real plan. I won't make growers settle a workplace argument while their seed is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 a full thinking system could choose seed substitutes, read every certificate and answer the grower cheaper than our office. The warehouse still has people moving bags until robots around 2031, but my job is a screen and phone job. I cannot turn eight years of order knowledge into a guaranteed warehouse wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the date from the card and ask for written notice and actual paid openings. I'd tell Salma that her restaurant work is hands-on for longer, though its bookings and ordering change in 2028. Publicly I'd ask the company to fund training before it cuts people, and I'd ask what help families can actually claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my desk role to end or lose most of its hours by 2028. Salma's confirmed shifts cannot cover the mortgage, food and the children's costs, and we have only three weeks saved. I would lie awake wondering which bill I could postpone without hurting the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the seed laboratory for a paid two-day trial collecting and labelling physical samples. I'd complete it only if the lab offers a real supervisor and safety instruction, and my current shift can be covered. We'd stop the planned garden patio before paying its deposit and put that money toward mortgage cash. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my desk job ends, I'd apply for a posted sample-handling role only if its wage with Salma's confirmed hours covers mortgage, food and child care; otherwise I'd search the few local employers and check support eligibility before putting any payment in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I know how to try new tools, but a three-week reserve gives no room for a wrong paid move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does lab work escape the thinking system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The sample reports and schedules could change in 2028, while hands-on collection lasts until robots around 2031 in this picture. I'd need actual paid physical duties and training, not a laboratory title. I don't know whether a place will open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the patio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we can use the old table this summer. I wouldn't say their home is in danger before I know if my wage stops. Salma and I would handle the mortgage conversation together.

fieldNote: His **2028 desk risk** precedes physical sample work facing robots around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me see whether I can handle samples before AGI takes our office decisions in 2031. Physical collection faces robots around 2034, while laboratory reports and ordering change with AGI. A paid trial is worth doing, but I would not call a lab badge a second career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our company for paid practice and a list of real sample-handling vacancies. I'd tell Salma we should try to build three months of cash before my desk changes. To growers I'd say a human still answers for a wrong bag today, even if software helps us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could move to sample work if a paid post exists and the wage meets our bills; I can't pay the mortgage with an interesting course. The five-year span could let me save, although Salma's shifts vary and our reserve starts at three weeks. I would still be worried about the desk and the later robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd complete a paid monthly sample-collection day if the lab manager approves and safety training fits around school pickup. I'd set aside 25 weekly from my pay only when Salma's confirmed shifts and my wage cover mortgage, food and childcare, aiming toward three months of cash. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd take a posted physical sampling role only if combined pay covers those bills; otherwise I'd search other local work while my desk notice runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years gives a real chance to practise. The money problem does not vanish with a longer calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn first in the lab?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn how to label a sample so a grower doesn't get another field's result. I'd watch the technician take a germination count before doing one myself. A bag of seed can look identical and still be the wrong promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is 25 a week enough to reach three months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on its own, no. We'd need steadier shifts or a raise, and I won't count either until it arrives. Twenty-five is a start that won't make us miss the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years puts me at 53, our children at nineteen and twenty-three. I would like to have a smaller mortgage, but with three weeks saved now I cannot promise that. The desk still faces AGI in 2036 and physical sample work faces robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company to fund training while people still have wages. I'd ask other managers to name the actual paid roles, not just give staff a course list. I'd tell Salma we need a plan for the mortgage that works even in a quiet restaurant month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might build a three-month reserve if both incomes hold, then pay extra on the mortgage. I still expect my desk work to change in 2036, and a lab post is not certain or permanent. The decade helps because I can learn and save while the current wage exists, even if it is low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year I'd ask for a funded seed-sampling certificate with paid practice days and complete it only if the firm agrees and school pickup is covered. I'd put 50 monthly into cash while our confirmed wages cover mortgage, food and child costs, pausing when Salma loses shifts. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd apply for a posted physical seed-testing job only if its wage with Salma's confirmed hours covers those bills; if there is none, I'd keep searching with the reserve while robots remain about three years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the household, though I can see more choices with ten years. Three weeks of cash is still where we start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you repay the mortgage faster now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd build a real buffer first. A quiet restaurant month can empty the account before the next payment. Only after three months saved would I consider extra repayments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm will not fund the certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my paid order work and ask another employer about a genuine trainee vacancy before spending our own money. I won't buy a certificate to hang over an empty fridge. The children need a working budget more than a new label for me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the one. My order decisions could go before I can build cash or qualify for physical seed testing, and Salma's restaurant shifts do not cover the mortgage alone. A written notice, a paid training place tied to an actual vacancy and time to test that work would help. If public support exists and we qualify, I'd use it, but I won't write an unknown amount into our budget.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the grower what happens when a substitute bag arrives after the soil is prepared. A perfect delivery plan cannot make late seed sprout last week. I want someone who can answer the phone when a field is waiting.

headlineQuote: A perfect delivery plan cannot make late seed sprout last week.
portrait: Tomas, **43**, manages six seed-order workers at a large company and uses AI daily for first delivery plans.
He has **eight years' experience** and a bachelor's degree, with ordinary skill but lower pay and few nearby seed offices.
He and Salma have **two school-age children** and a mortgage, with three weeks saved after a boiler replacement.
Fast AGI threatens his **desk wage**; he would test paid physical seed work only with a vacancy, training and enough household pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his seed-order wage before cash or a new qualification is ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and paid training tied to a real seed-testing vacancy.
Public help only if **eligibility is confirmed**, with no assumed payment in the household budget.
